newsitem.title: USA: Panel says Perot should not be in U.S. debates.
newsitem.headline: Panel says Perot should not be in U.S. debates.

text.p: A commission planning for the 1996 presidential debates recommended on Tuesday that Reform Party candidate Ross Perot be excluded from debates between President Bill Clinton and Republican Bob Dole.

The recommendation, based on the panel's assessment that the Texan billionaire did not have a realistic chance of winning, was immediately challenged by angry Perot aides, who said they would file a federal lawsuit later this week.

The Clinton camp also objected to the call, saying it still backed Perot's participation and would still press for his inclusion. But Dole, who had feared a strong showing by Perot would cost him support, welcomed the recommendation.

The Commission on Presidential Debates said in a statement: "The commission unanimously agreed with the unanimous recommendation of our independent advisory committee that only President Clinton and Senator Dole and their running mates be invited to participate."

The statement by commission co-chairmen Paul Kirk and Frank Fahrenkopf said: "Our decision ... was made on the basis that only President Clinton and Senator Dole have a realistic chance as set forth in our criteria to be elected the next president of the United States."

The bipartisan panel said it could reconsider its decision for later debates -- three or four are in prospect -- if Perot improved his weak position in opinion polls. Surveys show him with only five to eight percent support this year.

Four years ago, when Perot played a prominent role in the debates and went on to win about 19 percent of the popular vote, many Republicans claimed he took votes away from then-President George Bush and helped elect Democrat Clinton.

Dole spokesman Nelson Warfield said the decision "makes it a hell of a lot more likely" that the Republican candidate will win the election. And Dole, who is struggling badly in the polls, said on his arrival in Phoenix, Arizona for a campaign event that the debates should start quickly.

"I think the debates ought to begin, the 25th, 26th of this month rather than trying to crowd them all into October," he said. "I want to reach out to the Perot supporters ... I think we (Republicans) are the Reform party," Dole said.

The first debate had tentatively been scheduled for September 25 but Clinton asked for a delay because he is speaking to the United Nations General Assembly the day before and wanted more time to prepare for both appearances.

Asked if the Clinton campaign accepted the recommendation that Perot be excluded, Commerce Secretary Mickey Kantor, representing Clinton, said: "No." He added: "We believe that his participation is in the public interest."

Kantor, speaking before meeting with Republican officials to discuss the format of the debates, said: "We respect the debate commission but regret their recommendation and we'll begin discussions this afternoon about all the issues surrounding these debates. Everything is on the table."
At a campaign stop in Westland, Michigan, Clinton said he had enjoyed debating Perot in 1992. Asked whether he was worried about debating Dole one-on-one, he said: "I'm not afraid of any debate."

Russell Verney, National Coordinator of Perot's campaign, told reporters: "We will seek a temporary restraining order against the debates occurring until we can get a full and fair hearing." The law suit should be ready to be in U.S. District Court in Washington on Thursday or Friday, he said.

In 1992, Texas billionaire Perot ran as an independent candidate financing his own presidential campaign and took part in the debates. His third-placed election finish was one of the strongest by a third-force challenger in U.S. history.

This year, he formed his own Reform Party and named maverick economist Pat Choate as his running mate. On the basis of his strong 1992 showing, Perot qualified for $29.2 million in federal money to finance his 1996 presidential run.
So far, however, Perot has garnered only single-digit support in opinion polls that place Clinton and Dole far ahead of him and Clinton well out front of Dole.
The debates have become highlights of the presidential election seasons and a record 97 million Americans watched the final 1992 televised debate.
